title: Respiratory system
summary: How does air get in, and how are gases exchanged and carried?
cards.0.h: What does the respiratory system do?
cards.0.p: The respiratory system carries out gas exchange. It passes O2 from the air into the blood and removes CO2 from the blood. Every cell makes its own ATP through cellular respiration.
cards.0.svg#3: takes in O₂, gives off CO₂
cards.0.svg#12: the organ exchanges gases, and every living cell
cards.0.svg#13: (including lung cells) makes its own ATP
cards.0.key: The respiratory system does not make ATP. Glucose is broken down in the mitochondria of cells. Blood carries the gases between the lungs and the cells.
cards.0.once.soru: What is the main job of the respiratory system?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: The respiratory system passes O₂ into the blood and removes CO₂.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Every cell makes its own ATP through cellular respiration.
cards.1.h: The path of air: from nose to alveolus
cards.1.p: Air passes through the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles, in that order, to reach the alveoli. When you swallow, the epiglottis closes the larynx.
cards.1.svg#3: shared path of air and food
cards.1.key: Cartilage rings hold the trachea and bronchi open. Bronchioles have no cartilage, and smooth muscle takes its place. The vocal cords are in the larynx.
cards.1.etk.soru: Put in order the path the air you breathe takes to the alveolus.
cards.2.p: The capillaries in the airways warm the air, and the moist surface moistens it. Hairs and mucus filter out dust. Cilia sweep the mucus toward the pharynx.
cards.2.key: When you breathe through your mouth, most of this preparation is skipped. That is why breathing through your nose is healthier.
cards.2.once.soru: In winter you breathe cold air through your nose. How does the air reach the alveoli?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: The capillaries and moist surface of the nose and airways prepare the air.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: The airways warm and moisten the air before it reaches the alveoli.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Besides filtering, the airways also warm and moisten the air.
cards.3.p: The right lung has 3 lobes and the left lung has 2, because the left side makes room for the heart. The two-layered pleura around the lung and the fluid between its layers reduce friction.
cards.3.svg#2: front view, the heart sits in the notch on the left
cards.3.key: Thanks to the pleural fluid, the lung stays stuck to the chest wall and expands with it.
cards.3.once.soru: Can the lungs expand with their own muscles?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: The lungs have no skeletal muscle. Muscles expand the chest, and the lungs follow.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: The lungs cannot contract and relax on their own.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: Even in a deep breath, it is the chest and abdominal muscles that expand the chest.
cards.4.p: When you breathe in, the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles contract. The chest volume increases, the pressure drops below atmospheric pressure and air flows in. At rest, breathing out happens passively.
cards.4.svg#20: forced exhale: internal intercostals and abdominal muscles contract
cards.4.key: In a forced exhale, the internal intercostal muscles and the abdominal muscles contract. In this case, breathing out becomes active.
cards.5.p: In a calm breath, about 500 mL of air moves in and out, and this is called the tidal volume. The tidal volume plus the reserve volumes is called the vital capacity, which is about 4600 mL. 1200 mL of residual air always stays in the lungs.
cards.5.svg#8: total ≈ 5800 mL · approximate for an adult
cards.5.key: With effort you can breathe in 3000 mL more and breathe out 1100 mL more. Residual air is not part of the vital capacity.
cards.5.once.soru: Sitting calmly, about how much air do you take in with one breath?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: A calm breath is about 500 mL.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: That is close to the deepest breath possible. A calm breath takes in much less air.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: That is far too little, only about a sip of water.
cards.6.h: The alveolus: the gas exchange surface
cards.6.p: Hundreds of millions of alveoli have a total surface of about 70 m2, and their walls are one cell thick. O2 passes into the blood and CO2 into the alveolus by diffusion, driven by partial pressure differences.
cards.6.svg#11: partial pressures in mmHg, gases diffuse from high to low
cards.6.key: No ATP is used in this exchange. Surfactant lowers surface tension, so the alveoli do not collapse and stick together.
cards.7.p: Cells in the tissues use O<sub>2</sub> and make CO<sub>2</sub>. So in the tissue, PO<sub>2</sub> is low and PCO<sub>2</sub> is high. O<sub>2</sub> passes from the blood to the cells, and CO<sub>2</sub> from the cells to the blood.
cards.7.svg#10: in tissue: O₂ from blood to cell, CO₂ from cell to blood
cards.7.svg#11: blood circulates through the heart, the diagram is simplified
cards.7.key: In the alveolus, O₂ enters the blood, and in the tissue it leaves the blood. Partial pressure decides which way a gas moves.
cards.7.once.soru: Blood from the lungs has a PO₂ of 100, and a working muscle has 20 mmHg. Where does O₂ go?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: A gas diffuses from where its partial pressure is high to where it is low.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: PO₂ is lower in the muscle, so O₂ goes there.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: As long as there is a pressure difference, diffusion continues.
cards.8.p: About 98.5% of O2 is carried bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells. When PO2 is low, CO2 is high, or the surroundings are warm or acidic, hemoglobin releases O2 easily.
cards.8.svg#6: O₂ is released by: low PO₂, high CO₂,
cards.8.key: One hemoglobin binds 4 molecules of O₂. Fetal hemoglobin binds O₂ more tightly and takes O₂ from the mother's blood in the placenta.
cards.9.p: About 70% of CO2 is carried in plasma as bicarbonate (HCO3−). The enzyme carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells quickly combines CO2 with water.
cards.9.svg#10: in the lungs the reaction reverses and CO₂ is breathed out
cards.9.key: About 23% of CO₂ binds to hemoglobin, and 7% dissolves in plasma. When CO₂ rises in the blood, the blood becomes more acidic.
cards.10.p: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas that comes from badly burning stoves or water heaters. It binds to hemoglobin about 200 times more tightly than O2. So the blood cannot carry O2.
cards.10.svg#14: CO binds to Hb ~200 times more tightly than O₂
cards.10.svg#15: sources: stoves, water heaters, exhaust · colorless, odorless
cards.10.key: The signs of poisoning are headache, dizziness and loss of consciousness. There is enough hemoglobin, but it cannot carry O₂ because CO is bound to it.
cards.10.once.soru: A badly burning stove is in a closed room. Everyone has a headache. What should be done first?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: In CO poisoning, the first step is to ventilate. Then oxygen is given and medical help is called.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: While asleep you keep breathing in CO, which is very dangerous.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: A painkiller does not remove CO from the blood.
cards.11.p: The breathing rhythm is set by the medulla in the brainstem, and the pons fine-tunes it. The strongest trigger for breathing is a rise in CO2 in the blood. When CO2 rises, the pH drops, and breathing gets faster and deeper.
cards.11.svg#13: exercise: muscles make more CO₂ → breathing speeds up
cards.11.key: Chemoreceptors are found in the aorta, the carotid artery and the medulla. When you hold your breath, what pushes you to breathe is CO₂ building up more than a lack of O₂.
cards.12.p: During exercise, CO2 rises and breathing and heart rate speed up. At high altitude, the air is still 21% O2, but because air pressure is low, PO2 falls. Over time, the number of red blood cells in the blood increases.
cards.12.key: The hormone EPO, released by the kidney, increases red blood cell production. Climbers adjust by waiting a few days at altitude, which is called acclimatization.
cards.13.p: In asthma the bronchioles narrow, and in bronchitis the bronchi become inflamed. In COPD the airways narrow permanently, and in pneumonia the alveoli fill with fluid. Smoking damages the cilia.
cards.13.svg#18: Smoking: damages cilia, mucus builds up, gives off CO,
cards.13.svg#19: the main cause of COPD and lung cancer
cards.13.key: Asthma is usually reversible, but COPD is permanent. Smoking is the main cause of COPD and lung cancer.
cards.13.once.soru: Why does a smoker cough in the morning?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Because the cilia are damaged, mucus cannot be swept away and builds up. The body removes this mucus by coughing.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: Smoking does not make the lungs grow. It damages the airways.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: The cough comes from built-up mucus, not from blood.
cards.14.p: When you run, CO<sub>2</sub> rises and the medulla speeds up breathing. Adrenaline speeds up the heart. When water is lost through sweat, the kidneys hold on to water under the effect of the hormone ADH. The systems keep the internal balance together.
cards.14.key: Most of these controls are negative feedback. That means a change triggers a response that corrects it.
cards.14.once.soru: Your breathing speeds up when you run. Which system speeds up too?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: The heart speeds up, and more blood and oxygen go to the muscles.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: While running, less blood goes to digestion.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: The reproductive system has no such role in exercise.
cards.15.p:
• The respiratory system exchanges gases, and cellular respiration makes ATP.
• The airways warm, moisten and filter the air.
• When the diaphragm contracts, chest volume increases, pressure drops and air flows in.
• Gases cross by diffusion, driven by partial pressure differences.
• O2 is mostly carried by hemoglobin, and CO2 mostly as bicarbonate.
cards.15.svg#8: cellular respiration: ATP made in mitochondria
quiz.0.q: A person has a tidal volume of 450 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 2500 mL, an expiratory reserve volume of 1000 mL and a residual volume of 1200 mL. What is their vital capacity in mL?
quiz.0.e: Vital capacity is the tidal volume plus the two reserve volumes. 450 + 2500 + 1000 = 3950 mL. Residual air cannot be breathed out, so it is not added to this total.
quiz.1.q: During an asthma attack, the airway narrows most in the bronchioles. Why?
quiz.1.o.2: Bronchiole walls are lined with thick cartilage rings.
quiz.1.e: Cartilage rings hold the trachea and bronchi open. Bronchioles have no cartilage. In asthma, when the smooth muscle of the bronchiole contracts, the airway narrows easily.
quiz.1.y.1: More mucus adds to the narrowing. But the main cause is the contraction of smooth muscle in a wall with no cartilage.
quiz.1.y.2: It is the opposite, because cartilage keeps the airway open. The bronchiole can narrow because it has no cartilage.
quiz.1.y.3: Gas exchange happens in the alveolus. The narrowing of the bronchiole comes from the smooth muscle in its wall.
quiz.2.q: Put each change that happens at rest under breathing in or breathing out.
quiz.2.e: When you breathe in, the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract. The ribs rise, the volume increases, the pressure drops and air flows in. At rest, breathing out is passive. The muscles relax, the volume decreases and the pressure rises.
quiz.3.q: At the start of a capillary, PO<sub>2</sub> = 100 and PCO<sub>2</sub> = 40 mmHg. At its end, PO<sub>2</sub> = 40 and PCO<sub>2</sub> = 45 mmHg. Where is this capillary most likely to be?
quiz.3.e: The blood in this capillary has lost O<sub>2</sub> and gained CO<sub>2</sub>. This happens in tissues where O<sub>2</sub> is used. In the alveolus the opposite happens.
quiz.3.y.0: Around the alveolus, blood takes in O₂ and PO₂ rises. Here PO₂ falls, so this is a tissue capillary.
quiz.3.y.1: The pulmonary vein is not a capillary and carries oxygenated blood. A drop in PO₂ shows that O₂ is being given to a tissue.
quiz.3.y.2: The trachea is an airway, not a blood capillary. If PO₂ falls and PCO₂ rises, the capillary is in a working tissue.
A:ozet: Follow the air from the nose to the alveolus, work the breathing muscles, climb a mountain, exchange gases and make hemoglobin release O₂.
A:adimlar.0.metin: The air you breathe passes through a series of tubes from the nose to the alveolus. The pharynx is a path for both air and food. Make a guess first, then follow the air.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which one does air not pass through?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Air passes from the pharynx to the larynx, and from there into the trachea. The vocal cords are in the larynx.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The esophagus is the path for food. When you swallow, the epiglottis closes the larynx. When you breathe in, the epiglottis is open and air goes to the trachea.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The trachea splits in two. Each bronchus enters a lung and branches into bronchioles. So air does pass through the bronchus.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Work both muscles and take air in.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: When the diaphragm flattens, the chest expands downward. When the external intercostals contract, the chest expands up and out.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: The chest expanded both downward and up and out. When the pressure dropped below atmospheric pressure, air flowed in on its own.
A:adimlar.2.metin: At sea level, air pressure is 760 mmHg and 21% of air is O₂. So the partial pressure of O₂ is 760 × 0.21 ≈ 160 mmHg. Climb the mountain and cut PO₂ in half.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: Air pressure drops as you go higher. Climb until PO₂ is around 80 mmHg.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: At about 5.5 km, both air pressure and PO₂ drop by half, and PO₂ is about 80 mmHg. The O₂ share is still 21%.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The walls of the alveolus and the capillary are one cell thick. Gases move from where their partial pressure is high to where it is low. Make a guess first, then press play.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: Blood arriving at the capillary has a PO₂ of 40, and the alveolus has 100 mmHg. Where does O₂ go?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The partial pressure of O₂ is higher in the alveolus, so O₂ diffuses into the blood. CO₂ is higher in the blood (45 mmHg) and passes into the alveolus. No ATP is used.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A gas moves from where its partial pressure is high to where it is low. PO₂ is lower in the blood, so O₂ comes into the blood.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Gas exchange is diffusion and needs no energy. The driving force is the partial pressure difference.
A:adimlar.4.metin: As PO₂ falls, hemoglobin releases O₂. Make hemoglobin release more than half of the O₂ it carries.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: In resting tissue, PO₂ is 40 mmHg and hemoglobin releases only 1 O₂ there. A working muscle uses O₂ much faster.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: In a working muscle, PO₂ drops to 10-20 mmHg and hemoglobin releases most of its O₂. In resting tissue it releases only 1 O₂, and the rest stays in reserve.
A:adimlar.5.metin: CO₂ made in the tissue passes into the blood and is carried to the lungs. The enzyme carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells quickly combines CO₂ with water. Make a guess first, then press play.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: In what form is most CO₂ carried in the blood?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: About 23% of CO₂ binds to hemoglobin. Most CO₂ is carried in another form.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Only about 7% of CO₂ dissolves in plasma as a gas.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Carbonic acid splits into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ ions, and bicarbonate passes into the plasma. In the lungs the reaction reverses and CO₂ is breathed out.
A:adimlar.6.metin: CO₂ in the blood controls breathing. Faster breathing removes more CO₂. While running, your muscles' CO₂ production has tripled. Adjust your breathing and keep PCO₂ at 40.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.ipucu: The CO₂ removed must equal the CO₂ produced. If you breathe too fast, too much CO₂ is removed.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: When breathing tripled, as much CO₂ was removed as was produced. So PCO₂ stayed at 40 and the pH stayed at 7.4.
A:kapanis.0: Air passes through the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to reach the alveolus. The epiglottis keeps food out of the trachea.
A:kapanis.1: When the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, chest volume increases, pressure drops and air flows in.
A:kapanis.2: Gases cross by diffusion, driven by partial pressure differences. At altitude, it is the partial pressure of O₂ that drops, not its share.
A:kapanis.3: Most O₂ is carried by hemoglobin. Hemoglobin releases O₂ in tissues where PO₂ is low.
A:kapanis.4: Most CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate. Breathing is sped up mainly by a rise in CO₂ in the blood.
